text:
Evidence supports the mismatch, although direct studies of supervised item-transition counts are limited. [CatBoost](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.09516) demonstrates that target-inclusive statistics can encode an example’s own label and fail to generalize, especially for rare categories. Analogous graph evidence: [SpotTarget](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00899) identifies overfitting and distribution shift when training target edges appear in the graph but evaluation edges do not, with sparse nodes particularly affected. Applied to transition counts: a positive singleton transition guarantees its own support during training; an unseen next-item transition receives zero support at inference. This application is an inference from those findings.

Leave-one-user-out counts, C₋ᵤ(a,b)=C(a,b)−Cᵤ(a,b), remove all contributions from the target user, measuring independent collaborative support. User-grouped cross-fitting builds each training fold’s graph from other users; inference uses all permitted training histories. These are methodological extensions rather than established guarantees for sequential recommendation. [Scikit-learn’s cross-fitting demonstration](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/preprocessing/plot_target_encoder_cross_val.html) shows how excluding examples from their feature statistics reduces overfitting. User exclusion also removes legitimate earlier personal evidence; chronological construction instead preserves available history while excluding later events. [Ji et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11060) show that ignoring global chronology changes recommendation accuracy and model rankings. User exclusion alone cannot prevent temporal leakage.

Useful diagnostics: compare inclusive versus user-excluded support; report validation HR@10 separately for zero-support and supported transitions, plus their frequencies; ablate the count feature. Counts alone cannot distinguish destinations with zero pair support, so unseen-transition generalization requires other sequence, embedding, or higher-order signals. Keep the pinned benchmark splits unchanged; treat chronological graph variants as training-feature experiments, with gains determined by held-out validation rather than inflated training support.
